original.title: The Iron Cage Revisited: Institutional Isomorphism and Collective Rationality in Organizational Fields

core_idea: Organizations in the same field (universities, hospitals, NGOs, banks) tend to become more alike over time. DiMaggio and Powell argue this is often not because the shared form is the most efficient, but because looking like the others brings legitimacy. They name three pressures that produce this sameness: coercive (rules and demands from the state, donors or parent organizations), mimetic (copying peers that seem successful when the way forward is uncertain) and normative (shared standards spread by professions and education).
key_concepts_note: Use the concepts already stored for this theory in the library (theories.concepts).
when_to_use: Why do organizations in one sector adopt the same policies, structures or reforms (e.g. quality-assurance units in universities, gender policies in NGOs)?
Why does what an organization says it does (formal policy) differ from what it actually does?
How do donor, state or professional pressures shape organizations in a developing or post-Soviet context?
Typical data: organizational documents and policies, interviews with managers and staff, comparison across several organizations in one field.
common_mistakes: Saying 'isomorphism' without naming which of the three mechanisms is at work, and what evidence shows it.
Assuming that adopting a policy means implementing it. Check for decoupling between formal structure and daily practice.
Using the theory to explain how individuals change institutions without adding a strand built for agency (institutional work or institutional entrepreneurship).
Treating Meyer & Rowan (1977) and DiMaggio & Powell (1983) as the same argument: the first is about myth, ceremony and decoupling, the second about why organizations become alike.

work.title: Institutionalized Organizations: Formal Structure as Myth and Ceremony

development.adds: Organizations adopt formal structures as 'myth and ceremony' to look legitimate, and often decouple them from the actual work.

work.title: The Role of Institutionalization in Cultural Persistence

development.adds: Micro-level view: the more institutionalized a behaviour, the more it is taken for granted and the longer it persists.
Organizations do not just conform: they can acquiesce, compromise, avoid, defy or manipulate institutional pressures.

strengths.point: Gives a ready vocabulary for the gap between formal policy and real practice (decoupling), which is common in reform and donor-funded settings.

source.title: Institutionalized Organizations: Formal Structure as Myth and Ceremony

strengths.point: A mature, widely used lens for organization-level and field-level questions, so there is a large body of studies to compare your findings with.

critiques.point: The 'new' institutionalism became too structural and lost the attention to action and interests of the 'old' institutionalism; the authors argue the two should be reconciled.

source.title: Ending the Family Quarrel: Toward a Reconciliation of “Old” and “New” Institutionalisms

critiques.point: Better at explaining sameness and stability than change. If actors are shaped by institutions, how do they change them? Later work had to add agency explicitly.
